quorum auctores non potes non odisse. iam nunc uolumus suggerere de artibus et de his, quorum, auctores in nominibus exsecramur. scimus nihil esse nomina mortuorum, sicut nec ipsa simulacra eorum; sed thought_title: Theater as shared property of Venus and Bacchus
orientation: Tertullian has just traced the circus and chariot racing to idolatrous founders, and now turns to the theater, arguing that its very location, titles, and arts belong to Venus and Bacchus.
pass_a_gloss: First Erichthonius dared to yoke the chariot and the four horses and to stand victorious on swift wheels. Let us pass to theatrical matters, whose origin common and titles equal according to the very naming of the games from the beginning and administration joined with the equestrian affair we have already shown. The apparatus also is shared from that part, by which one goes to the stage from temples and altars and that ill-omened use of incense and blood amid flutes and trumpets, with two most polluted arbiters of funerals and sacrifices, the dissignator and the haruspex. Thus when we passed from the origins of the games to the circus games, from there we shall now direct ourselves to the theatrical games. From the fault of its location the theater is properly a shrine of Venus. In this way at last this kind of work emerged in the world. For often the censors were destroying theaters just as they were being born, stitching them up with morals, whose great danger from wantonness they foresaw, so that already here it may turn out as testimony to the pagans, their own opinion making common cause with us, and to us for the heightening of discipline even human prerogative. And so Pompey the Great, less than his own theater alone, when he had built that citadel of all foulnesses, fearing at some time the censorial censure of his memory, placed a temple of Venus on top and calling the people by edict to the dedication named it not a theater but a temple of Venus, under which, he said, we have placed the steps of the shows. Thus he veiled a work condemned and to be condemned with the title of a temple and mocked discipline with superstition. But it suits Venus and Bacchus. Those two demons are conspired and sworn together with each other, of drunkenness and lust. And so the theater of Venus is also the house of Bacchus. For they also used to call other theatrical games properly Liberalia, besides being devoted to Bacchus, which are Dionysia among the Greeks, also instituted by Bacchus. And clearly in the theatrical arts too there is the patronage of Bacchus and Venus. The things that are private and proper to the stage, of gesture and bending of the body, they sacrifice to the softness of Venus and Bacchus, dissolved, the one through sex, the other through extravagance. But the things that are carried on by voice and by modes and by instruments and by writings have Apollos and Muses and Minervas and Mercuries as their owners. You should hate, Christian, those whose authors you cannot not hate. Now we wish to suggest about the arts and about those whose authors we curse in their names. We know that the names of the dead are nothing, just as not even their images themselves; but we do not ignore who under those names and instituted images work and rejoice and feign divinity, the worthless spirits, namely, demons. We see therefore that even the arts are dedicated to the honors of those who inhabit the names of their authors, and that they are not free from idolatry, whose institutors are for that reason also held as gods. Rather, as far as it pertains to the arts, we ought to have perceived more deeply that demons from the beginning foreseeing for themselves among the other defilements of idolatry also the pollutions of the shows, by which they might call man away from the Lord and bind him to their own honor, inspired also the talents of arts of this kind. For neither would it have been procured by others what was going to come to them, nor would they have published them through other men then than through those very ones, in whose names and images and histories they determined to carry on for themselves the business of the deceit of consecration. So that the order may be completed, let us also enter upon a review of the contests.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the plural noun phrase; 'matters' preserves the general scope rather than narrowing to 'plays' or 'stage'.
The glossary does not cover this term; 'softness' is the literal sense and carries the effeminacy Tertullian condemns.
Literal sense of luxus as excess or luxury, paired with sex as the two vices of Bacchus and Venus.
Manceps is literally a purchaser or contractor who owns a right; 'owners' conveys the proprietary claim of the gods over the arts.
Nequam means worthless or wicked; 'worthless spirits' is literal and matches Tertullian's contempt for demons.
Literal genitive phrase; 'deceit' preserves the active deception Tertullian attributes to demons.

pass_b_english: Let us now turn to theatrical matters. We have already shown that the theater shares its origin with the games, and that its titles are equal to theirs, since from the beginning the very name and administration of the games were joined with the equestrian affair. Its apparatus is also a partner from that side, since the way to the stage leads from temples and altars and that unhappy business of incense and blood, amid flutes and trumpets, under two most polluted arbiters of funerals and sacrifices: the dissignator, who arranges the funeral procession, and the haruspex, who inspects the entrails of sacrificial victims. So when we passed from the origins of the games to the circus, we will now direct our course from there to the theatrical games.

Because of the vice of its location, the theater is properly a shrine of Venus. This is how that kind of work finally emerged into the world. For often the censors were destroying theaters just as they were being born, since they foresaw the immense danger from their wantonness. So here already the pagans' own judgment may serve as testimony, agreeing with us and giving us, for the heightening of discipline, even a human prerogative. And so Pompey the Great, lesser than his theater alone, when he had built that citadel of every foulness, fearing at some point the censorial censure of his memory, placed a temple of Venus on top and, calling the people to the dedication by edict, named it not a theater but a temple of Venus. 'Under it,' he said, 'we have placed the steps for the shows.' Thus he covered a work condemned and still to be condemned with the title of a temple, and mocked discipline with superstition.

But Venus and Bacchus are well matched. Those two demons are conspirators and sworn allies of drunkenness and lust. Therefore the theater of Venus is also the house of Bacchus. For they used to call other theatrical games properly Liberalia, devoted to Bacchus beyond the rest—those which among the Greeks are Dionysia, also instituted by Bacchus. And clearly in the theatrical arts too there is the patronage of Bacchus and Venus. The things that are private and proper to the stage—gesture and the bending of the body—they sacrifice to the softness of Venus and Bacchus, dissolved through sex and through extravagance. But the things carried out by voice and melody and instruments and writings have Apollos, Muses, Minervas, and Mercuries as their servants. Hate, O Christian, the things whose authors you cannot help but hate.

Now we want to speak about the arts and about those whose authors we curse in their names. We know that the names of the dead are nothing, just as their images themselves are nothing; but we are not ignorant of who operates under those names and instituted images, and rejoices and feigns divinity—namely worthless spirits, demons. We see therefore that even the arts are dedicated to the honors of those who inhabit the names of their authors, and that they are not free from idolatry, since their founders are for that very reason considered gods. Indeed, as far as the arts are concerned, we ought to have understood more deeply that the demons from the beginning, foreseeing for themselves among the other pollutions of idolatry also the defilements of the shows, by which they might call man away from the Lord and bind him to their own honor, inspired the talents of such arts as well. For what was going to come to them would not have been procured by others, nor would they have published it through other men then than through those very ones in whose names and images and histories they determined to carry out for themselves the business of the deceit of consecration. So that the order may be completed, let us also enter upon a review of the contests.
notes: The source text contains apparent OCR damage: 'apparatus ? ł\ratus' and 'mo.ţis' and 'per- \' agatur' and 'LLiberi'. The gloss renders the legible sense without inventing text; 'apparatus' is read as the noun, 'modis' is inferred from 'mo.ţis' as modes, 'peragatur' from 'per- agatur', and 'Liberi' from 'LLiberi'.

problems.quote: stitching them up for the sake of morals
problems.why: Latin says censors destroyed theaters, not that they stitched them up; the English adds a detail not in the source.
problems.fix: remove "stitching them up for the sake of morals," rendering: "censors destroyed theaters ..."
problems.ruling: moribus consuentes means 'accustomed to morals'; 'stitching them up' is unsupported and misleading.

edits.old: For often the censors were destroying theaters just as they were being born, stitching them up for the sake of morals, since they foresaw the immense danger from their wantonness.
edits.new: For often the censors were destroying theaters just as they were being born, since they foresaw the immense danger from their wantonness.

fixed: Removed 'stitching them up for the sake of morals' because the Latin 'moribus consuentes' means 'consulting for morals' (i.e., acting for the sake of morals), not 'stitching them up'; the censors destroyed theaters, they did not stitch them up.

problems.quote: have Apollos and Muses and Minervas and Mercuries as their owners
problems.source_quote: Apollines et Musas et Mineruas et Mercurios mancipes habent
problems.why: Latin says the arts have these deities as "mancipes" (servants/slaves), not as owners; agency is reversed.
problems.fix: have Apollos, Muses, Minervas, and Mercuries as their servants
problems.ruling: Latin 'mancipes habent' means arts have deities as guarantors/contractors, not owners; translation reverses agency.

edits.old: have Apollos and Muses and Minervas and Mercuries as their owners
edits.new: have Apollos, Muses, Minervas, and Mercuries as their servants

fixed: The Latin 'mancipes' means servants or slaves, not owners, so the agency was reversed; corrected to 'servants'.

last_rejected.quote: those whose authors we curse in their names
last_rejected.source_quote: de his, quorum, auctores in nominibus exsecramur
last_rejected.why: Source means 'about those whose authors we curse by their names'; English reads as if the authors curse in their own names.
last_rejected.fix: about those whose authors we curse by their names
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'auctores in nominibus exsecramur' = we curse authors by name; English matches this meaning.

last_rejected.quote: Pompey the Great, lesser than his theater alone, when he had built that citadel of every foulness
last_rejected.source_quote: Pompey ... solo theatro suo minor cum illam arcem omnium turpitudinum extruxisset
last_rejected.why: English reverses the relationship, implying Pompey is lesser than his theater; Latin says his theater was smaller than the citadel he built.
last_rejected.fix: Pompey the Great, whose own theater was smaller when he built that citadel of all foulness, ...
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'solo theatro suo minor' means Pompey was 'less than his theater alone'—a rhetorical point, not a size comparison with the citadel.

polish.changed: Removed the misplaced repetition of the Erichthonius sentence from section 9, clarified the roles of the dissignator and haruspex, and smoothed sentence order and pronoun references for modern readers while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.why: Two Roman offices with no explanation; reader cannot place them.
notes.fix: Gloss: 'the dissignator (funeral director) and the haruspex (diviner from entrails)'

notes.why: Obscure term for a type of farce; unexplained.

notes.quote: Erichthonius was the first who dared to yoke four horses to a chariot and stand victorious upon its swift wheels. Let us now turn to theatrical matters.
notes.why: Repeats verbatim from section 9; appears to be a misplaced repetition before the new topic.
notes.fix: Remove the repeated sentence or mark as recapitulation.
